title: BridgeCast: Bridging Ocean Wave Forecasts to Reanalysis via Flow Matching with Exogenous Variables

paper.title: BridgeCast : Bridging Ocean Wave Forecasts to Reanalysis via Flow Matching with Exogenous Variables
paper.abstract: Abstract Ocean wave forecasting is essential for maritime safety, offshore operations, and coastal resilience, yet remains challenging due to systematic biases in physics-based models. Physical models, while widely used, rely on approximations and parameterizations that limit their accuracy under complex ocean-atmosphere conditions. To enhance ocean wave forecasting, we propose BridgeCast , within a physics-AI hybrid framework for bias correction. BridgeCast is a probabilistic model based on conditional flow matching (CFM) that learns to transform physical model forecasts into reanalysis-like fields. It treats physical forecasts as corrupted observations and employs a continuous-time generative process to bridge their distribution toward that of reanalysis data. BridgeCast is parameterized by a Transformer-based architecture that enables spatiotemporal modeling, incorporation of exogenous atmospheric variables, and flexible inference via both ordinary and stochastic differential equation formulations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that BridgeCast consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across regions and forecast lead times.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Ocean wave forecasting is critical for maritime safety, offshore operations, energy infrastructure, hazard mitigation, and coastal resilience ( Sun et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) . At present, operational wave forecasts are predominantly generated by physics-based numerical models, such as the spectral wave model WaveWatch-III ( WW3 ) ( Tolman, 2009 ) , which is often forced by atmospheric forecasts from the Global Forecast System ( GFS ) operated by the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP), and the WaveModel ( WAM ) ( ECMWF, 2023 ) used within the Integrated Forecasting System ( IFS ) operated by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). These models simulate the evolution of the wave energy spectrum through governing equations that account for wind forcing, nonlinear wave-wave interactions, and dissipation processes. While grounded in well-established physical principles and widely used in practice, they inevitably rely on approximations, parameterizations, and imperfect boundary conditions, leading to systematic biases and reduced accuracy under complex or rapidly changing ocean-atmosphere conditions such as storms. For example, Fig. 1 (left column) shows the forecast errors of GFS-WW3 in the Gulf of Mexico and North Sea in 2025 (lead-time: 30 h), varying within ± \pm 0.8m (RMSE: 0.29) and ± \pm 2.0m (RMSE: 0.67). These errors are substantial and may lead to critical misjudgments, posing safety risks for maritime and coastal operations. Figure 1: An illustration of BridgeCast ’s process of bridging GFS-WW3 ’s forecasts to the reanalysis data of ERA5 in (a) Gulf of Mexico, and (b) North Sea. The numbers in brackets are RMSEs. τ \tau is flow time. “Ours” is BridgeCast , which resembles ERA5 with less errors than GFS-WW3 . To correct the biases of the physical forecasters, we introduce a physics-AI hybrid framework that improves their outputs using a novel deep learning model, BridgeCast . BridgeCast is a probabilistic predictor designed to bridge the distribution of physical model forecasts to that of reanalysis data using conditional flow matching (CFM) ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) . Reanalysis data, such as those provided by the ECMWF Reanalysis 5th Generation ( ERA5 ) ( Hersbach et al., 2020 ) , are generated through data assimilation that integrates observational data and are widely used as a proxy for ground truth in evaluating oceanic and atmospheric forecasts due to their consistency and reliability ( Hersbach et al., 2020 ; Sharmar and Markina, 2020 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . BridgeCast treats physical model forecasts as “corrupted images”, which serve as conditions for a generative model based on continuous-time stochastic processes, enabling the generation of more accurate reanalysis-like outputs. Fig. 1 illustrates the transport from GFS-WW3 forecasts to the ERA5 distribution by BridgeCast , where τ \tau is the flow time, “Ours” refers to bias-corrected forecasts, and ERA5 represents the reanalysis data. BridgeCast progressively refines a perturbed forecast ( τ = 0 \tau=0 ) and ultimately reduces forecasting errors, producing outputs that closely resemble reanalysis fields. To our knowledge, BridgeCast is among the first to apply CFM for bias correction in physical models for ocean wave forecasting, and can serve as a plug-and-play module for existing operational systems ( e.g. , GFS-WW3 , IFS-WAM ) within a physics-AI hybrid framework that inherits the advantages of physical modeling while mitigating their limitations through “learning to bridge” distributions. Additionally, BridgeCast is parameterized by a novel two-head Diffusion Transformer ( DiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) ) encoder-decoder capable of (1) spatiotemporal modeling of the geoscientific data; and (2) incorporating of exogenous variables such as atmospheric forcing factors that have a critical impact on ocean dynamics. Moreover, BridgeCast supports inferences using either an ordinary differential equation (ODE) formulation for efficient computation or a stochastic differential equation (SDE) formulation for uncertainty-aware forecasting, providing flexibility depending on practical requirements. In summary, our contributions are as follows. • We investigate a physics-AI hybrid framework and study the problem of correcting biases in physical models for ocean wave forecasting using deep learning-based CFM. • We propose BridgeCast , a novel CFM-based probabilistic model that bridges the distribution of forecasts from physical models and that of reanalysis data. BridgeCast adopts a Transformer-based architecture supporting spatiotemporal modeling, exogenous variables, and flexible inference. • We conduct comprehensive experiments using GFS , IFS , and ERA5 data, and compare BridgeCast with state-of-the-art (SOTA) deterministic and probabilistic baselines, demonstrating its superior performance across different regions and lead times.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Bias Correction for Ocean Wave Forecasting . Bias correction and statistical post-processing have become increasingly important in ocean wave forecasting. Early studies focused on statistical and operational correction techniques ( Vannitsem et al., 2021 ) . Later works extended these ideas through spatiotemporal correction frameworks and climate-aware calibration methods ( Ai et al., 2022 ; Lira Loarca et al., 2023 ) . Recent advances increasingly employ deep learning models ( Sun et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) . For example, ( Sun et al., 2022 ) introduced a BU-Net architecture for correcting GFS-WW3 forecasts; ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) utilized TrajGRU ( Shi et al., 2017 ) with wind-wave coupled inputs for real-time correction; ( Lira Loarca et al., 2023 ) applied U-Net and Transformer components to improve medium- and long-range wave forecasts. Related studies have further explored physics-informed corrections and upstream atmospheric adjustments ( Meisner et al., 2023 ; Peduto et al., 2025 ) . Despite these advances, most existing learning-based approaches ( Sun et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) rely on deterministic regression objectives and do not explicitly model conditional forecast distributions or transport dynamics, leaving generative approaches such as flow matching underexplored for ocean wave forecast bias correction. Earth System Predictions . Recent data-driven Earth models are mostly for weather and climate forecasting. Representative global forecasting systems include deterministic models ( Lam et al., 2023 ; Pathak et al., 2022 ) that aim to emulate or replace weather prediction at global scales. Precipitation nowcasting models ( Shi et al., 2015 ; Sønderby et al., 2020 ; Ribeiro and Pucer, 2026 ) focus on rapid prediction of weather events. Foundation-style Earth system models such as Earthformer ( Gao et al., 2022b ) , ClimaX ( Nguyen et al., 2023 ) , and NeuralGCM ( Kochkov et al., 2024 ) extend these capabilities toward multi-variable, multi-task modeling of the Earth system. Emerging probabilistic ( Gong et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ) , latent-variable ( Leinonen et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) , and diffusion-based approaches ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) further explore generative formulations. However, these models are primarily designed for global weather or Earth system variables and are not tailored for ocean wave forecasting. Flow-Based Models . Traditional continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) ( Chen et al., 2018 ) model data via neural ODEs, but require costly numerical integration, which can be prohibitive for high-dimensional spatiotemporal applications. CFM ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) and Rectified Flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) methods address this limitation by directly regressing a time-dependent vector field against a conditional probability path, avoiding the need for solving ODEs during training. Unlike diffusion models, which rely on stochastic denoising processes that typically require many iterative sampling steps, CFM enables learning ODE trajectories that transport noise to data more efficiently. FlowCast ( Ribeiro and Pucer, 2026 ) is a recent example that applies CFM to precipitation nowcasting. More recently, stochastic interpolants ( Albergo et al., 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2025a ) have been proposed as a unified framework connecting diffusion models and flow-based formulations. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to adapt CFM-based modeling to ocean wave forecast correction with explicit spatiotemporal modeling and exogenous variable conditioning.

sections.heading: 3 The Proposed BridgeCast Model
sections.text: Problem Statement . Bias correction for ocean wave forecasts is framed as an image sequence correction task with exogenous variables. In this task, a physical model generates a forecast of wave variables — which are endougenous variables — 𝒳 = [ 𝐗 1 , … , 𝐗 T ] \mathcal{X}=[{\bf X}_{1},...,{\bf X}_{T}] within a forecast horizon of length T T , where 𝐗 t ∈ ℝ H × W × C {\bf X}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C} ( 1 ≤ t ≤ T 1\leq t\leq T ) is a forecasted image with C C channels ( i.e. , variables) at time step t t . Additionally, we are given observed atmospheric variables — which are exogenous variables — 𝒵 = [ 𝐙 1 , … , 𝐙 T ′ ] \mathcal{Z}=[{\bf Z}_{1},...,{\bf Z}_{T^{\prime}}] within a time window of length T ′ T^{\prime} , where 𝐙 t ′ ∈ ℝ H ′ × W ′ × C ′ {\bf Z}_{t^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times C^{\prime}} ( 1 ≤ t ≤ T ′ 1\leq t\leq T^{\prime} ) is an image with C ′ C^{\prime} channels at time step t ′ t^{\prime} . It is noteworthy that 𝒳 \mathcal{X} and 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} can have different lengths and sizes. The goal is to predict wave variables within the physical model’s forecasting horizon 𝒴 ^ = [ 𝐘 ^ 1 , … , 𝐘 ^ T ] \hat{\mathcal{Y}}=[\hat{{\bf Y}}_{1},...,\hat{{\bf Y}}_{T}] where 𝐘 ^ t ∈ ℝ H × W × C \hat{{\bf Y}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C} , such that 𝒴 ^ \hat{\mathcal{Y}} is closer to the reanalysis data 𝒴 = [ 𝐘 1 , … , 𝐘 T ] \mathcal{Y}=[{\bf Y}_{1},...,{\bf Y}_{T}] than the physical model’s raw output 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . Preliminaries . BridgeCast is built upon CFM ( Albergo et al., 2025b ) , which defines a conditional distribution p τ ​ ( x τ | x 0 , x 1 ) p_{\tau}(x_{\tau}|x_{0},x_{1}) , typically a Gaussian distribution with mean ( 1 − τ ) ​ x 0 + τ ​ x 1 (1-\tau)x_{0}+\tau x_{1} and time-dependent standard deviation σ τ \sigma_{\tau} , where 0 ≤ τ ≤ 1 0\leq\tau\leq 1 . This distribution establishes a bridge that interpolates between a source data sample x 0 ∼ p 0 x_{0}\sim p_{0} and a target data sample x 1 ∼ p 1 x_{1}\sim p_{1} . It basically defines a stochastic process x τ = ( 1 − τ ) ​ x 0 + τ ​ x 1 + σ τ ​ ϵ x_{\tau}=(1-\tau)x_{0}+\tau x_{1}+\sigma_{\tau}\epsilon , where ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,{\bf I}) , that can bridge two arbitrary distributions p 0 p_{0} and p 1 p_{1} ( Albergo et al., 2025a ) . CFM trains a velocity field v 𝜽 ​ ( x , τ ) v_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(x,\tau) by regressing it against the velocity target d ​ x τ d ​ τ \frac{dx_{\tau}}{d\tau} . Additionally, the framework trains a denoiser function s 𝜽 ​ ( x , τ ) s_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(x,\tau) by regressing it against the sampled Gaussian noise ϵ \epsilon . Next, we specify the proposed BridgeCast under the CFM framework ( § \lx@sectionsign 3.1 ), and introduce our parameterization of v 𝜽 ​ ( x , τ ) v_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(x,\tau) and s 𝜽 ​ ( x , τ ) s_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(x,\tau) ( § \lx@sectionsign 3.2 ).

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Datasets. We evaluate BridgeCast using public real-world oceanic and atmospheric data, including (1) ERA5 (ECMWF ReAnalysis, 5th generation) ( Hersbach et al., 2020 ) ; (2) GFS (Global Forecast System) ( Zhou et al., 2019 ) ; and (3) IFS (Integrated Forecasting System) ( Richardson, 2000 ) . ERA5 provides reanalysis data about ocean and atmosphere in different regions, which are often considered as accurate and used as ground truth for assessing different forecasting models ( Hersbach et al., 2020 ; Sharmar and Markina, 2020 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) (note: ERA5 does not perform forecasting). Both GFS and IFS provide wave and atmospheric forecasts by physical models for different regions, but they differ in physical models. Dataset Region N train N_{\text{train}} N val N_{\text{val}} N test N_{\text{test}} Dimension GFS Gulf of Mexico 193,944 2,904 2,904 33 × 47 33\times 47 North Sea 193,896 2,904 2,904 32 × 48 32\times 48 California Coast 192,240 2,904 2,904 35 × 41 35\times 41 IFS Gulf of Mexico 29,520 17,376 17,184 33 × 47 33\times 47 North Sea 29,520 17,376 17,184 32 × 48 32\times 48 California Coast 29,520 17,376 17,184 35 × 41 35\times 41 The collected GFS data is available between 2021 and 2025 (3hr per frame), which is split into train (2021-2023)/validation (2024)/test (2025) sets. The IFS data is available between 2024 and 2025 (3hr per frame), which is split into train (2024)/validation (2025/1-2025/6)/test (2025/7-2025/12) sets. For both, there are 4 wave variables ( e.g. , wave height, direction) and 11 atmospheric variables ( e.g. , winds, pressure). Samples are generated by segmenting the data into 24-frame windows ( i.e. , 72hr) with stride 2 for GFS and stride 4 for IFS . GFS ’s validation and tests use stride 24 to compose an evaluation of non-overlapped sample windows. It is noteworthy that each sample may be forecasted by a physical model T l ′ T_{l}^{\prime} hrs ahead ( 3 ≤ T l ′ ≤ 168 3\leq T_{l}^{\prime}\leq 168 ), leading to a lead-time T l ∈ [ 3,240 ] T_{l}\in[3,240] for individual frames in a sample window. We categorize the lead-time into Short-Term ( 3 ≤ T l ≤ 24 3\leq T_{l}\leq 24 ), Mid-Term ( 24 < T l ≤ 72 24<T_{l}\leq 72 ), and Long-Term ( 72 < T l ≤ 240 72<T_{l}\leq 240 ) for evaluation in three regions – Gulf of Mexico, North Sea, and California Coast. The ERA5 data covers these periods and are used for model training and evaluation. The resolution of each frame is 0.5 ∘ 0.5^{\circ} . The Table above summarizes the datasets, where N train N_{\text{train}} / N val N_{\text{val}} / N test N_{\text{test}} are the number of frames in train/validation/test set. More details about the datasets can be found in Appendix C.3 . The Compared Methods . We compare BridgeCast with the SOTA methods, including the vanilla physical models: (1) GFS-WW3 ( Tolman, 2009 ) , (2) IFS-WAM ( ECMWF, 2023 ) ; deterministic models: (3) U-Net ( Ronneberger et al., 2015 ) , (4) EarthFormer ( Gao et al., 2022b ) , (5) EarthFarseer ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , (6) SimVP ( Gao et al., 2022a ) , (7) AFNO ( Guibas et al., 2022 ) , (8) TimeXer ( Wang et al., 2024 ) ; and probabilistic models: (9) FlowMatch ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) , (10) DiffCast ( Yu et al., 2024 ) , (11) FlowCast ( Ribeiro and Pucer, 2026 ) . Among them, TimeXer is a recent time series model that can explicitly encode both endogenous variables and exogenous variables. For other baselines, we concatenate the wave and atmospheric variables in their inputs. We trained the baselines to correct physical model’ biases as our method does except for FlowMatch which was trained to reconstruct ERA5 data without conditioning on physical forecasters. Comparing with it can highlight the importance of bridging physical models to reanalysis. For our BridgeCast , we present its performance using both SDE ( ε SDE ≠ 0 \varepsilon_{\text{SDE}}\neq 0 in Algorithm 2 ) and ODE ( ε SDE = 0 \varepsilon_{\text{SDE}}=0 ) inferences, leading to two variants BridgeCast -s ( i.e. , SDE) and BridgeCast -o ( i.e. , ODE). The parameter σ \sigma is grid-searched within [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , ε SDE \varepsilon_{\text{SDE}} is grid-searched within ( 0 , 0.1 ] (0,0.1] (for a small noise) using validation set. More details about the methods and their parameter settings can be found in Appendix C.2 . The implementation details are deferred to Appendix C.5 . Evaluation . Following ( Ribeiro and Pucer, 2026 ) , we evaluate wave forecasting by widely used metrics, including Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) , threshold-weighted CRPS (twCRPS) ( Fricker et al., 2013 ) , Critical Success Index (CSI) ( Schaefer, 1990 ) , and Heidke Skill Score (HSS) ( Heidke, 1926 ) . RMSE and CRPS measure forecasting errors, thus a small value is preferred. CSI and HSS measure hit ratio of correct predictions, thus a larger value is better. They are particularly useful for detecting extreme events ( e.g. , storm). twCRPS is the threshold-weighted CRPS at the 95th percentile that also fits event detection. Details about the evaluation metrics can be found in Appendix C.1 .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we proposed BridgeCast within a physics-AI framework for ocean wave forecasting. BridgeCast learns to bridge physics-based forecasts toward that of reanalysis data through a CFM process. The proposed Transformer-based architecture supports spatiotemporal modeling, exogenous variable encoding, and flexible ODE/SDE inference. Extensive experiments on GFS , IFS , and ERA5 datasets demonstrate that BridgeCast outperforms SOTA deterministic and probabilistic baselines across different lead times and different regions. These results highlight the potential of BridgeCast for improving operational geoscientific forecasting systems as a flexible plug-and-play module. Additionally, we defer our discussion of limitation and future directions to Appendix A .

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations
sections.text: Two Inference Modes . The proposed BridgeCast has two inference methods, including SDE-based inference ( ε SDE ≠ 0 \varepsilon_{\text{SDE}}\neq 0 ), leading to BridgeCast -s, and ODE-based inference ( ε SDE = 0 \varepsilon_{\text{SDE}}=0 ), leading to BridgeCast -o. BridgeCast -s is suitable for probabilistic forecasting but is less efficient than BridgeCast -o, which also supports probabilistic forecasting through random initial perturbations. While the proposed model support the two approaches based on application requirements, it cannot provide the advantage of both methods simultaneously. A future work is to investigate the trade-off between efficiency and uncertainty modeling for a balanced development. Inadequate Modeling of Look-Back Windows . The proposed BridgeCast correct biases of physical models instantly. The current design has not yet incorporated the historical wave and atmospheric data as look-back windows for forecasting-style bias correction. Due to the temporal dependency such as periodicity in the data, modeling look-back windows together with physical model outputs and exogenous variables may provide further improvement, which remains open for further exploration.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare BridgeCast against nine representative baselines spanning deterministic spatiotemporal forecasters and probabilistic generative models, all trained on the same paired ( 𝒳 , 𝒵 , 𝒴 ) (\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{Y}) tuples and evaluated under the same protocol. The deterministic baselines cover four major architectural families relevant to gridded geoscience forecasting. U-Net ( Ronneberger et al., 2015 ) is the canonical encoder–decoder convolutional baseline, configured with base channel width 64 (GFS) or 32 (IFS) to match training-set size. SimVP ( Gao et al., 2022a ) uses depthwise-separable spatial–temporal convolutional blocks for parameter-efficient video prediction. AFNO ( Guibas et al., 2022 ) replaces self-attention with adaptive Fourier neural operators and is the standard spectral-mixing baseline used in modern weather emulators (e.g. FourCastNet). EarthFormer ( Gao et al., 2022b ) introduces cuboid attention along factorized spatial and temporal axes; we use the [ 4 , 4 , 4 ] [4,4,4] cuboid configuration tuned for regional grids. EarthFarseer ( Wu et al., 2024 ) augments a SimVP-style backbone with a Fourier-Transformer (FoTF) module to capture long-range dependencies; it is our most parameter-heavy deterministic baseline ( ∼ \sim 25.6 M). TimeXer ( Wang et al., 2024 ) is a transformer that explicitly separates exogenous (atmospheric) and endogenous (wave) channels through cross-attention with a residual prediction head — the closest deterministic analog to our two-head design. The probabilistic baselines fall into two families. DiffCast ( Yu et al., 2024 ) is a denoising diffusion model trained from Gaussian noise to the target distribution with 1000 training steps and 250-step DDIM sampling at inference; we use its standard U-Net backbone with channel multipliers ( 1 , 2 , 4 ) (1,2,4) . FlowCast is a Conditional Flow Matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) variant we construct on top of an EarthFormer backbone, sampled with a 10-step Euler ODE solver; it shares the bridge-style training objective with BridgeCast but uses a Gaussian source rather than a forecast-anchored source. BridgeCast is comparable in parameter count to FlowCast and lighter than DiffCast and EarthFarseer. This places BridgeCast ’s gains squarely on the modeling side rather than on raw scale.

sections.heading: GFS-Wave (primary).
sections.text: We use the operational NCEP GFS-Wave (WAVEWATCH III) forecast ( Tolman, 2009 ) , taking all four daily initialization cycles (00, 06, 12, 18 UTC) and extracting four wave channels: significant wave height (SWH), mean wave period (MWP), and mean wave direction encoded as ( sin ⁡ θ d , cos ⁡ θ d ) (\sin\theta_{d},\cos\theta_{d}) to avoid the 0 / 2 ​ π 0/2\pi discontinuity. GFS-Wave is distributed at 0.5 ∘ 0.5^{\circ} on the regional crops we use, matching the ERA5 wave grid which is produced only at 0.5 ∘ 0.5^{\circ} ( Hersbach et al., 2020 ) . The regional GFS-Wave archive begins in March 2021 and bounds the GFS training-set size.

sections.heading: IFS-WAM (cross-system).
sections.text: We additionally use ECMWF IFS-WAM forecasts ( ECMWF, 2023 ) from the public ECMWF open-data archive at 00 and 12 UTC, lead times 0 , 3 , … , 240 0,3,\ldots,240 h. Native IFS-WAM resolution is 0.25 ∘ 0.25^{\circ} ; we stride-2 subsample to 0.5 ∘ 0.5^{\circ} on the same regional bounding boxes as GFS-Wave so the input grid is bit-identical to the GFS training grid. For both systems, window-start leads lie in [ 3,168 ] [3,168] h, and evaluation lead-time bands extend to 240 h. The IFS open-data archive begins 2024-03-01, which limits the IFS training budget to roughly one seventh of the GFS budget — a deliberate stress test of the corrector in the small-data regime.

sections.heading: Atmospheric exogenous 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} .
sections.text: For each forecast system, atmospheric fields are taken from the same forecast cycle and lead time as the wave forecast and regridded to the wave grid before training, so 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} and 𝒳 \mathcal{X} share an identical H × W H{\times}W spatial extent and no spatial resampling occurs inside the network. 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} contains C ′ = 11 C^{\prime}=11 channels: raw 10 m wind components ( u 10 , v 10 ) (u_{10},v_{10}) and mean sea-level pressure (msl), plus eight deterministic derivations chosen to make wind-forcing physics visible to the network — 10 m wind speed, wind direction ( sin , cos ) (\sin,\cos) , u 10 2 u_{10}^{2} , the per-frame finite-difference time derivatives of u 10 u_{10} , v 10 v_{10} , and msl, and the wind-forcing magnitude u 10 2 + v 10 2 u_{10}^{2}+v_{10}^{2} . The derived channels are mathematically redundant given the raw fields but accelerate convergence on the small training budgets used here, following the inductive-bias argument made by CorrDiff ( Mardani et al., 2025 ) for its derived input fields. 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} enters BridgeCast as conditioning only and is never part of the supervised target.

sections.heading: Target 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} .
sections.text: The supervised target is the corresponding ERA5 wave field ( Hersbach et al., 2020 ) at the same valid times and the same 0.5 ∘ 0.5^{\circ} grid, with the same four channels. ERA5 wave variables are assimilated against altimeter and buoy observations and are the standard reference for wave-model verification.

sections.heading: Study regions.
sections.text: We evaluate on three coastal regions spanning different wave climates: the Gulf of Mexico ( 15.0 15.0 – 31.0 ∘ 31.0^{\circ} N, 98.0 98.0 – 75.0 ∘ 75.0^{\circ} W; grid 33 × 47 33{\times}47 ; ≈ 0.85 \approx 0.85 ocean), a fetch-limited basin dominated by tropical cyclones; the North Sea ( 48.0 48.0 – 63.5 ∘ 63.5^{\circ} N, 4.0 ∘ 4.0^{\circ} W– 19.5 ∘ 19.5^{\circ} E; grid 32 × 48 32{\times}48 ; ≈ 0.78 \approx 0.78 ocean), an extratropical-storm regime with the highest baseline GFS-Wave errors of the three; and the California coast ( 30.0 30.0 – 47.0 ∘ 47.0^{\circ} N, 135.0 135.0 – 115.0 ∘ 115.0^{\circ} W; grid 35 × 41 35{\times}41 ; ≈ 0.81 \approx 0.81 ocean), a long-fetch swell regime in which the raw forecast is already comparatively strong and residual-correction gains are hardest to obtain. Land cells are excluded from every loss and every metric, for BridgeCast and for every baseline.

sections.heading: Sample geometry.
sections.text: Each sample is a trajectory of T = 24 T=24 frames at Δ ​ t = 3 \Delta t=3 h, starting at forecast lead ℓ ∈ [ 3,168 ] \ell\in[3,168] h. Frame index s ∈ { 0 , … , T − 1 } s\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\} has valid forecast lead T l , s = ℓ + s ​ Δ ​ t T_{l,s}=\ell+s\Delta t . The trajectory length is fixed across samples, while the window-start lead varies. Individual frames are assigned to the lead-time bands defined below, whose upper boundary is 240 h.

sections.heading: Lead-time conditioning: one model, all leads.
sections.text: BridgeCast trains a single model jointly across forecast lead times, conditioning on a per-frame valid-lead encoding ℓ ~ s = ( ℓ + s ​ Δ ​ t ) / ℓ max \tilde{\ell}_{s}=(\ell+s\Delta t)/\ell_{\max} , where ℓ max = 168 \ell_{\max}=168 h denotes the maximum window-start lead. This encoding is supplied to AdaLN-Zero alongside the interpolant time τ \tau .

sections.heading: Lead-time sampling rationale.
sections.text: Operational use of marine forecasts concentrates at short leads (next-day decisions for shipping, port operations, offshore work, and fisheries dominate query traffic). A uniform-in- ℓ \ell training distribution would over-represent long leads relative to where forecast skill matters in deployment. We therefore sample ℓ ∼ log ⁡ 𝒰 ⁡ [ 3,168 ] \ell\sim\log\,\mathcal{U}[3,168]\, h on the 3 h grid, which (i) concentrates training mass in proportion to operational utility and (ii) acts as importance-sampling reweighting of the joint loss across leads — the same role that non-uniform timestep sampling plays in modern diffusion training, where it has been shown to reduce gradient variance and accelerate convergence ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ) . GFS-Wave (NOMADS, 0.5 ∘ 0.5^{\circ} , four daily cycles since March 2021) materializes the ℓ \ell -sampler at export time: ℓ ∼ log ⁡ 𝒰 ⁡ [ 3,168 ] \ell\sim\log\,\mathcal{U}[3,168]\, h is drawn independently per cycle, yielding a variable count of trajectories per cycle (mean ≈ 2.3 \approx 2.3 , range 1–10). The variability reflects the per-cycle stochastic draw and the constraint that cycles late in the archive period drop trajectories at long ℓ \ell where the ERA5 target window extends past the cache end. Validation and test use a 72 h non-overlapping initialization stride for independent samples. IFS-WAM (ECMWF Open Data via AWS public replica bucket, two daily cycles since 2024-03-01) is much smaller: the official ECMWF Open Data Portal retains only the most recent ∼ \sim 12 forecast runs, and the full MARS historical archive requires a commercial Service Agreement we do not hold. This caps the IFS training budget at roughly 1 / 7 1/7 the GFS budget. Given the small archive, we adopt deterministic per-cycle export with exactly two ℓ \ell draws per (00/12 UTC) initialization from the 3 h grid { 3 , 6 , … , 168 } \{3,6,\ldots,168\}\, h. Validation and test retain every available initialization; trajectories therefore overlap in valid time (median 3 h spacing), and test-set metrics aggregate over unique initialization times to avoid double-counting overlapping windows.

sections.heading: Lead-time bands.
sections.text: We report results in three operationally meaningful bands chosen a priori : Short-Term (3–24 h), Mid-Term (27–72 h), and Long-Term (75–240 h).

sections.heading: C.3.3 Splits and Sample Counts
sections.text: Splits are strictly chronological. For GFS-Wave: training 2021-03–2023-12, validation 2024, test 2025, yielding ∼ \sim 8,080 training trajectories per region (Gulf 8,081; NS 8,079; California 8,010) and 121 non-overlapping validation and 121 test trajectories per region. For IFS-WAM: training 2024-03–2024-12, validation 2025-01–2025-06, test 2025-07–2025-12, yielding 1,230 training, 724 validation, and 716 test trajectories per region. Normalization statistics are computed from the training split only and frozen for validation and test.

Physical models, while widely used, rely on approximations and parameterizations that limit their accuracy under complex ocean-atmosphere conditions. To enhance ocean wave forecasting, we propose BridgeCast , within a physics-AI hybrid framework for bias correction. BridgeCast is a probabilistic model based on conditional flow matching (CFM) that learns to transform physical model forecasts into reanalysis-like fields. It treats physical forecasts as corrupted observations and employs a continuous-time generative process to bridge their distribution toward that of reanalysis data. BridgeCast is parameterized by a Transformer-based architecture that enables spatiotemporal modeling, incorporation of exogenous atmospheric variables, and flexible inference via both ordinary and stochastic differential equation formulations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that BridgeCast consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across regions and forecast lead times. 1 Introduction Ocean wave forecasting is critical for maritime safety, offshore operations, energy infrastructure, hazard mitigation, and coastal resilience ( Sun et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) . At present, operational wave forecasts are predominantly generated by physics-based numerical models, such as the spectral wave model WaveWatch-III ( WW3 ) ( Tolman, 2009 ) , which is often forced by atmospheric forecasts from the Global Forecast System ( GFS ) operated by the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP), and the WaveModel ( WAM ) ( ECMWF, 2023 ) used within the Integrated Forecasting System ( IFS ) operated by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). These models simulate the evolution of the wave energy spectrum through governing equations that account for wind forcing, nonlinear wave-wave interactions, and dissipation processes. While grounded in well-established physical principles and widely used in practice, they inevitably rely on approximations, parameterizations, and imperfect boundary conditions, leading to systematic biases and reduced accuracy under complex or rapidly changing ocean-atmosphere conditions such as storms. For example, Fig. 1 (left column) shows the forecast errors of GFS-WW3 in the Gulf of Mexico and North Sea in 2025 (lead-time: 30 h), varying within ± \pm 0.8m (RMSE: 0.29) and ± \pm 2.0m (RMSE: 0.67). These errors are substantial and may lead to critical misjudgments, posing safety risks for maritime and coastal operations. Figure 1: An illustration of BridgeCast ’s process of bridging GFS-WW3 ’s forecasts to the reanalysis data of ERA5 in (a) Gulf of Mexico, and (b) North Sea. The numbers in brackets are RMSEs. τ \tau is flow time. “Ours” is BridgeCast , which resembles ERA5 with less errors than GFS-WW3 . To correct the biases of the physical forecasters, we introduce a physics-AI hybrid framework that improves their outputs using a novel deep learning model, BridgeCast . BridgeCast is a probabilistic predictor designed to bridge the distribution of physical model forecasts to that of reanalysis data using conditional flow matching (CFM) ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) . Reanalysis data, such as those provided by the ECMWF Reanalysis 5th Generation ( ERA5 ) ( Hersbach et al., 2020 ) , are generated through data assimilation that integrates observational data and are widely used as a proxy for ground truth in evaluating oceanic and atmospheric forecasts due to their consistency and reliability ( Hersbach et al., 2020 ; Sharmar and Markina, 2020 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . BridgeCast treats physical model forecasts as “corrupted images”, which serve as conditions for a generative model based on continuous-time stochastic processes, enabling the generation of more accurate reanalysis-like outputs. Fig. 1 illustrates the transport from GFS-WW3 forecasts to the ERA5 distribution by BridgeCast , where τ \tau is the flow time, “Ours” refers to bias-corrected forecasts, and ERA5 represents the reanalysis data. BridgeCast progressively refines a perturbed forecast ( τ = 0 \tau=0 ) and ultimately reduces forecasting errors, producing outputs that closely resemble reanalysis fields. To our knowledge, BridgeCast is among the first to apply CFM for bias correction in physical models for ocean wave forecasting, and can serve as a plug-and-play module for existing operational systems ( e.g. , GFS-WW3 , IFS-WAM ) within a physics-AI hybrid framework that inherits the advantages of physical modeling while mitigating their limitations through “learning to bridge” distributions. Additionally, BridgeCast is parameterized by a novel two-head Diffusion Transformer ( DiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) ) encoder-decoder capable of (1) spatiotemporal modeling of the geoscientific data; and (2) incorporating of exogenous variables such as atmospheric forcing factors that have a critical impact on ocean dynamics. Moreover, BridgeCast supports inferences using either an ordinary differential equation (ODE) formulation for efficient computation or a stochastic differential equation (SDE) formulation for uncertainty-aware forecasting, providing flexibility depending on practical requirements. In summary, our contributions are as follows. • We investigate a physics-AI hybrid framework and study the problem of correcting biases in physical models for ocean wave forecasting using deep learning-based CFM. • We propose BridgeCast , a novel CFM-based probabilistic model that bridges the distribution of forecasts from physical models and that of reanalysis data. BridgeCast adopts a Transformer-based architecture supporting spatiotemporal modeling, exogenous variables, and flexible inference. • We conduct comprehensive experiments using GFS , IFS , and ERA5 data, and compare BridgeCast with state-of-the-art (SOTA) deterministic and probabilistic baselines, demonstrating its superior performance across different regions and lead times. 2 Related Work Bias Correction for Ocean Wave Forecasting . Bias correction and statistical post-processing have become increasingly important in ocean wave forecasting. Early studies focused on statistical and operational correction techniques ( Vannitsem et al., 2021 ) . Later works extended these ideas through spatiotemporal correction frameworks and climate-aware calibration methods ( Ai et al., 2022 ; Lira Loarca et al., 2023 ) . Recent advances increasingly employ deep learning models ( Sun et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) . For example, ( Sun et al., 2022 ) introduced a BU-Net architecture for correcting GFS-WW3 forecasts; ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) utilized TrajGRU ( Shi et al., 2017 ) with wind-wave coupled inputs for real-time correction; ( Lira Loarca et al., 2023 ) applied U-Net and Transformer components to improve medium- and long-range wave forecasts. Related studies have further explored physics-informed corrections and upstream atmospheric adjustments ( Meisner et al., 2023 ; Peduto et al., 2025 ) . Despite these advances, most existing learning-based approaches ( Sun et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) rely on deterministic regression objectives and do not explicitly model conditional forecast distributions or transport dynamics, leaving generative approaches such as flow matching underexplored for ocean wave forecast bias correction. Earth System Predictions . Recent data-driven Earth models are mostly for weather and climate forecasting. Representative global forecasting systems include deterministic models ( Lam et al., 2023 ; Pathak et al., 2022 ) that aim to emulate or replace weather prediction at global scales. Precipitation nowcasting models ( Shi et al., 2015 ; Sønderby et al., 2020 ; Ribeiro and Pucer, 2026 ) focus on rapid prediction of weather events. Foundation-style Earth system models such as Earthformer ( Gao et al., 2022b ) , ClimaX ( Nguyen et al., 2023 ) , and NeuralGCM ( Kochkov et al., 2024 ) extend these capabilities toward multi-variable, multi-task modeling of the Earth system. Emerging probabilistic ( Gong et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ) , latent-variable ( Leinonen et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) , and diffusion-based approaches ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) further explore generative formulations. However, these models are primarily designed for global weather or Earth system variables and are not tailored for ocean wave forecasting. Flow-Based Models . Traditional continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) ( Chen et al., 2018 ) model data via neural ODEs, but require costly numerical integration, which can be prohibitive for high-dimensional spatiotemporal applications. CFM ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) and Rectified Flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) methods address this limitation by directly regressing a time-dependent vector field against a conditional probability path, avoiding the need for solving ODEs during training. Unlike diffusion models, which rely on stochastic denoising processes that typically require many iterative sampling steps, CFM enables learning ODE trajectories that transport noise to data more efficiently. FlowCast ( Ribeiro and Pucer, 2026 ) is a recent example that applies CFM to precipitation nowcasting. More recently, stochastic interpolants ( Albergo et al., 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2025a ) have been proposed as a unified framework connecting diffusion models and flow-based formulations. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to adapt CFM-based modeling to ocean wave forecast correction with explicit spatiotemporal modeling and exogenous variable conditioning. 3 The Proposed BridgeCast Model Problem Statement . Bias correction for ocean wave forecasts is framed as an image sequence correction task with exogenous variables. In this task, a physical model generates a forecast of wave variables — which are endougenous variables — 𝒳 = [ 𝐗 1 , … , 𝐗 T ] \mathcal{X}=[{\bf X}_{1},...,{\bf X}_{T}] within a forecast horizon of length T T , where 𝐗 t ∈ ℝ H × W × C {\bf X}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C} ( 1 ≤ t ≤ T 1\leq t\leq T ) is a forecasted image with C C channels ( i.e. , variables) at time step t t . Starting from an SDE-based formulation that defines a stochastic probability path, we derive a hybrid training objective combining CFM and diffusion-style score matching under a unified interpolant framework. Using SDE explicitly equips BridgeCast with the capability of representing the probabilistic structures of ocean and atmospheric data including uncertainty and stochastic variability through an explicit noise process. Following ( Ribeiro and Pucer, 2026 ) , we evaluate wave forecasting by widely used metrics, including Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) , threshold-weighted CRPS (twCRPS) ( Fricker et al., 2013 ) , Critical Success Index (CSI) ( Schaefer, 1990 ) , and Heidke Skill Score (HSS) ( Heidke, 1926 ) . RMSE and CRPS measure forecasting errors, thus a small value is preferred. CSI and HSS measure hit ratio of correct predictions, thus a larger value is better. They are particularly useful for detecting extreme events ( e.g. , storm). twCRPS is the threshold-weighted CRPS at the 95th percentile that also fits event detection.
